title: Konbini Pulse: Owner-Run Launch Verdict Panel
one_liner: A paid panel of convenience-store owners who report real shelf sell-through of new items in the first 48 hours after each Tuesday launch, sold to food makers who otherwise see only HQ's verdict.
customer: Small and mid-size food and beverage makers, including OEM and private-label suppliers and exclusive-item partners of the big three chains, at ¥150k-500k per brand per month. Later customers are ad agencies, trend and product-development teams, and investors who follow listed food companies.
problem: Every chain launches dozens to hundreds of new items on Tuesdays. An item's fate is effectively decided in 3-10 days, and HQ decides listing and delisting on its own data. The maker, who invested in a line, packaging and ingredients, sees only what HQ tells them. Owners see the real signal: stock-out times, leftover at closing, repeat buyers versus first-day curiosity, counter comments, and differences between office districts and residential areas. That information is never shared with the supplier. Makers cannot tell whether a delisting was fair, so they cannot negotiate.
solution: A 30-second phone routine for each owner: photograph the shelf at fixed times on days 1, 2 and 3, log leftover count at the disposal scan, and tap one of a few reasons customers gave. The panel of 40-150 stores across chains and neighborhoods is aggregated into a '48-hour verdict' delivered to the maker by Thursday: sell-through curve, sell-out time, leftover, repeat rate, and buyer profile by district type. It uses shelf observations and the owner's own counts, not HQ system exports, to reduce contractual risk. Owners are paid monthly, so the panel is a new income line that does not depend on royalty.
why_now: Ingredient and rice inflation has squeezed maker margins, so a failed launch is more expensive than before. SKU churn is accelerating. Japan's revised subcontract law, in force since January 2026, tightens buyers' duty to negotiate prices with commissioned manufacturers, so evidence has value in negotiations. Alternative-data buyers and product teams have no view into konbini shelves, because chain POS data is proprietary.
revenue_model: Subscription per brand, ¥150k-500k a month, plus ¥50k per launch report for smaller makers. Custom studies and delisting-defense reports cost ¥300k-1M. Owners receive ¥8-15k a month in cash plus a revenue share. Aggregate trend data is licensed to agencies and investors.
non_obvious_insight: Suppliers are structurally blind because the only party that counts their sales is the party that decides their fate. The owners standing at the shelf are the only independent observers, and they are invisible to the market because no one pays them. Once owners are paid to observe, the supplier's negotiating position changes. The moat is a trusted network of owners, not software. Data that comes from a shelf photo and a leftover count is less exposed to franchise confidentiality clauses than POS exports.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 stores across the three chains in Osaka through owner chat groups and the franchisee union, paying ¥10k a month each. Build a phone app that takes shelf photos on a schedule and captures counts in a few taps. Choose the next Tuesday launch wave and produce one '48-hour verdict' for five Osaka-area makers with konbini exclusives, offered at ¥50k per launch. Get legal review of the franchise contract clauses on data before scaling. Convert three makers to monthly subscriptions by day 90.

title: Amps Not Acres: Power Headroom for Retrofits
one_liner: Headroom reports and a load-sequencing kit that let plants add machines inside existing walls without a new transformer.
customer: Owners and plant managers of 20-300 employee manufacturers, and machine-tool, compressor and robot dealers who need to know whether a customer can power what they sell.
problem: Site selectors and economic developers think reshoring is limited by land, buildings and permits. The data say otherwise. Factory construction is down 22-32% from peak, yet nondefense capital-goods orders hit a record $85.9B in July, so equipment is going into old buildings. Transformer and switchgear prices are up 89-96% since 2019 as data centers compete for the same gear. Utility service upgrades cost six figures and take a year or more.
solution: Step 1 is a Headroom Report. It pulls 12 months of utility interval data (Green Button) and uses measured demand (NEC 220.87 allows this) to show how many kW can be added, ready for a PE stamp. Step 2 is a clamp-on CT and PLC/gateway kit that staggers compressors, furnaces, welders and spindle start-ups to cap demand peaks. Step 3 adds an optional battery or thermal-storage partner for the residual gap.
why_now: Record capital-goods orders with $953B unfilled, prices for electrical gear up sharply, and reshoring that is happening in existing buildings. No incumbent sells 'create amps in software' to a 50-person shop.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per report (dealers pay to close sales). $5-15k for hardware and install. $200-400 a month for monitoring. Referral fees from dealers and battery vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nameplate capacity is not the constraint. Measured coincident peak is, and it is usually far below service rating. The scarce input is amps, and amps can be created by sequencing loads.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 machine dealers on the report as a free pre-sale add-on. Get interval data from 5 plants. Partner with a licensed PE for stamping. Assemble the first controller from off-the-shelf CTs and a PLC.

title: All-In Site Quotes for Chassis-Free Homes
one_liner: Type a parcel address, get a fixed-price foundation, utility-hookup and permit package for a factory-built home, delivered by a local crew network.
customer: Manufactured and modular home dealers, small landowners and buyers, and factory builders that need site-work partners. Rural and small-town jurisdictions benefit indirectly.
problem: The ROAD to Housing Act (signed July 11, 2026) kills the steel-chassis rule, worth about $10K or 10% of unit cost, though HUD must still publish standards. Cheaper units will ship, but the sale is decided by unknown site costs: foundation, utilities, septic or well, set crew and permits. These stay local and human, and dealers cannot quote the all-in price.
solution: A parcel-level site-cost estimator using soils, flood zone, utility distance, jurisdiction fees and foundation type, returning a fixed-price quote in 24 hours. It is backed by a vetted crew network (excavation, foundation, set, utilities) on 7-day pay, one accountable contract, and packaged construction-to-perm financing. Begin with conventional manufactured homes on permanent foundations, so revenue starts before HUD standards land.
why_now: ROAD Act enacted July 2026 with HUD standards pending and a federal showcase of factory-built homes. Site work is exactly where the labor shortage and permit friction bite hardest. Standard duplex and townhome blueprints are being funded.
revenue_model: 10-15% GC margin on site packages ($30-60K). $300-500 quote fee credited on booking. Dealer referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone watching the ROAD Act watches factories and financing. The bottleneck will be the last 100 feet, and price uncertainty there kills the cheap-home pitch. The first team that gives a real all-in number becomes the dealers' default site partner and captures the margin the factory cannot.
first_30_days: Choose a county cluster in Texas or the Southeast where manufactured homes are common. Sign two dealers. Build the estimator from public GIS, flood and utility data. Deliver 20 free quotes and convert 2-3 to jobs with existing subs.

title: Rescue Orphaned Steno Notes With Stroke-Level AI
one_liner: A translation service that turns retired or deceased reporters' unreadable steno files into certifiable transcripts for stalled appeals, using a neural stroke-to-text model in place of the missing personal dictionary.
customer: County and state court administrators, public defender and appellate defender offices, and state AG appellate divisions. Secondary customers are retiring reporters and their estates. The first buyer is an appellate defender office with transcript orders stuck because the reporter left, paying about $2.50-$4 per page with a $1,500 minimum.
problem: Steno notes are a personal code, not a shared language. Another reporter cannot read them without the writer's dictionary, which holds phonetic strokes plus thousands of private shortcuts called briefs. When a reporter retires, dies or moves away, their untranscribed notes are effectively dead. Appeals stall for months, and courts may have to redo hearings or accept an inadequate record. Retention rules (California is 10 years for criminal cases and 5 for most others) mean old notes are also being boxed up or destroyed as reporters retire. The average reporter is in their mid-50s, and the workforce has shrunk about 21% in a decade.
solution: Train a stroke-sequence model. Input is the raw stroke stream with timestamps. Output is English with punctuation and Q/A structure. Training data comes from open steno corpora and community theory dictionaries, synthetic strokes with randomized personal-brief variation, and consented archives from retired reporters. Where the reporter also ran a backup audio recording, fuse audio and strokes to resolve homophones. Sell three products. (1) Rescue: per-page conversion, human-scoped by a retired reporter who certifies the transcript as prepared from the original reporter's notes. (2) Archive escrow: retiring reporters pay a one-time fee or a small monthly fee to have notes and dictionary converted, indexed and held by a custodian that satisfies retention rules. (3) Later, a scoping copilot for active reporters, who spend 1-3 hours editing per hour of testimony.
why_now: The 2026 retirement wave is here, and NCRA-cited data puts the average member age around 56. The 5-10 year retention windows for notes written in 2016-2021 are closing now. California's 2026 Supreme Court ruling (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) requires courts to give indigent litigants a verbatim record on request, which will create more appeals that need transcripts. Sequence models can now handle noisy phonetic-to-text conversion with context, and the open steno community (Plover) has published theory and dictionaries.
revenue_model: Per-page rescue fees, priced below the $4-6 ordinary transcript rate and paid by courts or appellate offices. Escrow and conversion packages for retirees (about $300-$800 one-time, or $25 per month). Annual contracts with court systems for backlog clearing. Later, a $99-$149 per month scoping copilot for active reporters, who already pay $3,000+ for CAT software.
non_obvious_insight: Only the writer can read steno notes. Court administrators do not track how many untranscribed notes sit with reporters about to retire. The stroke stream is also a cleaner input than audio, because a trained human already resolved the speaker, punctuation and homophones in real time. Almost nobody outside the profession knows the raw-notes problem exists.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 retired reporters through state association retiree lists. They donate or license old practice files and act as reviewers and certifiers. Build a baseline model on synthetic and open steno data, then test it blind on their files and record the accuracy. Cold-call 10 appellate defender and public defender offices with one question: do you have appeals stalled because the reporter is unavailable? Close 2-3 paid pilots at the $1,500 minimum.

title: Closed-School Science Labs Shipped to African Schools
one_liner: Take decommissioned lab benches, microscopes, fume hoods and Chromebooks from US schools being closed, refurbish them into container-sized lab packages with a practical-exam curriculum, and sell them to private secondary schools in East and West Africa.
customer: Buyers are private and faith-based secondary school networks in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria and Ghana, paying $8-15k per lab package. Sellers are US districts, charters and private schools that are closing and want fast, lawful disposal at low cost.
problem: More than 1,000 US public schools closed in 2025-26. Chicago alone has 135k empty seats, and Portland, Minneapolis and Albuquerque are queued behind it. Districts dispose of equipment through slow public-surplus auctions that recover pennies. Meanwhile African private schools running on tiny per-student budgets cannot afford lab equipment, even though national practical exams and newer competency-based curricula require it. A new lab costs $30-50k and takes months to import.
solution: Inventory soon-to-close buildings and remove complete science rooms, robotics kits, libraries and tested Chromebooks (with NIST-grade data wipes and export of working goods only). Bundle them into a 40-foot container with local installation, a practical-exam curriculum (matched to Kenyan, Nigerian or Ghanaian exam boards), a one-day teacher orientation, and a small annual refill of consumables. The district gets a disposal certificate and a possible donation receipt.
why_now: Closures are at a four-year high, so supply is predictable and geographically concentrated. The AI memory crunch, with memory now 30-40% of a device's bill of materials, has raised new-device prices and made used Chromebooks valuable. Distributed solar and batteries mean African schools can now run lab equipment and computers. As I understand it, Kenya's first competency-based senior-school cohort (2026) requires STEM practicals many schools cannot deliver.
revenue_model: Lab packages sell at $9-14k against a landed cost of $5-6k. A curriculum and refill subscription adds $600 per school per year. Districts pay a $1-3k decommissioning fee per closure in place of an auction consignment fee, or grant surplus title for free.
non_obvious_insight: A closing school is a fully assembled, curriculum-matched capital asset that public procurement can only sell by the pound, while the same asset is the binding constraint on practical-exam pass rates in low-fee African schools. The margin is in the bundle of equipment, practical curriculum and teacher orientation, not in the equipment, and that bundle is exactly what charity donation programs do not offer.
first_30_days: Pick one district and walk three soon-to-close buildings. Offer free removal of the first 10 science rooms in exchange for title to the equipment. Get letters of intent and 30% deposits from two or three African private-school owners through diaspora, church or school-association networks. Ship one container of two labs plus 200 tested Chromebooks. Line up an export broker and a data-wipe vendor before touching anything.

title: After-Hours Shop-Lab Leasing in Shrinking Schools
one_liner: A booking and insurance layer that rents idle high-school shops, labs and classrooms to apprenticeship programs, trade schools and microschools on nights and weekends.
customer: Declining-enrollment districts (facilities and business managers) and tenants: apprenticeship sponsors (JATCs, IEC and ABC chapters), Workforce Pell training providers, microschool operators.
problem: Chicago has 135k empty seats and more than 1,000 schools closed nationally in 2025-26. Districts are structurally slow to repurpose buildings and closures are politically toxic. Meanwhile trade programs need labs with power, ventilation and benches, and building their own costs millions.
solution: Inventory idle CTE shops, labs and gyms by the hour (power, ventilation, accessibility, parking), a standard license agreement with liability insurance and custodial and security add-ons, calendar and billing, and matching to tenants. Rent hours, not buildings, to avoid closure politics.
why_now: The enrollment cliff is squeezing budgets. Workforce Pell allows 49% of instruction to be outsourced for apprenticeship-linked programs, and data-center-driven electrician demand is growing training capacity needs.
revenue_model: 15-25% take of lab and classroom rent (typically $40-120 per hour) plus insurance and custodial add-on margin; optional district SaaS.
non_obvious_insight: The politically feasible move is not closing or selling but renting the hours between 4pm and 9pm. The tenants are already funded, and the district only has to approve a license, not a school closure.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 districts each with an underused shop or lab. Sign one apprenticeship sponsor as anchor tenant. Draft the standard license and insurance rider. List the first 10 rooms and measure rent per hour.

title: Human Baseline Vault for AI Detection
one_liner: Proctored, ID-verified, unassisted human writing and speech, timestamped and sealed, sold first as ground truth for detector calibration and later as low-background evaluation data.
customer: AI-detection vendors, ed-tech firms and publishers, university integrity offices, trust-and-safety teams, and AI labs' evaluation teams.
problem: Studies report detector false-positive rates of 5-20% on native English and up to 61% on non-native writing. 25+ universities have restricted detectors, and a February 2026 New York court ordered Adelphi to expunge a student's AI accusation. Vendors cannot prove error rates by population because clean post-2022 human ground truth is unknowable, since everyone's 'human' data may be AI-assisted.
solution: Recruit 20k+ verified people across strata (non-native English, neurodivergent, technical, legal and academic writers, age bands) to write and speak in proctored sessions. Samples are timestamped and hash-anchored. Sell calibration sets and per-population false-positive certificates to detector vendors, then an annually refreshed vault as 'low-background steel' for evaluations and future disputes.
why_now: Over half of web traffic is automated and training and evaluation sets are increasingly contaminated. Lawsuits and university bans mean detector buyers now need error rates by population, and AI labs need uncontaminated human evaluation data.
revenue_model: $50-250k dataset licences, $20-75k per detector audit and certificate, and annual refresh subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Like pre-1945 steel free of nuclear fallout, verified pre-contamination human data gets more valuable every year, and its value lies in the chain of custody, not the text itself.
first_30_days: Recruit 500 participants through two university partners for a native versus non-native pilot. Pitch two detector vendors and one ed-tech firm. Publish an independent study on false positives by population to earn press.

title: Water Due Diligence for Senior Housing Deals
one_liner: A 'Phase I for water' that grades a senior living property or CCRC bond on supply security, drought exposure, contamination compliance and in-building Legionella risk before lenders and buyers commit.
customer: HUD-232 and bridge lenders, senior-housing acquirers and Sunbelt developers, CCRC bond underwriters and muni credit analysts, and insurers. Pricing is $4-12k per deal report and $25-60k a year for portfolio subscriptions.
problem: Senior housing occupancy is 90.1%, the highest since 2007, and construction is the lowest since 2012 with a roughly $275B shortfall. New development will restart in Sunbelt states where Colorado River cuts (2027+), groundwater rules, PFAS and lead compliance, and drought restrictions bite. The asset class is uniquely exposed: 24/7 occupancy, heavy laundry, kitchens and cooling towers, frail residents you cannot evacuate, and Legionella that kills mostly older adults. CCRC bonds promise care for life on 30-year horizons, yet a standard environmental Phase I says nothing about water security.
solution: A standard report covering legally deliverable supply, the provider's source portfolio (river, groundwater, reuse), moratorium and curtailment history, a five-year rate outlook, PFAS, lead and nitrate compliance of the serving utility, and an in-building water-management-plan audit (Legionella per CMS and ASHRAE 188, cooling towers). It also covers drought-restriction impacts on operations and NOI sensitivity to a 30% water-cost spike. Output is a letter grade plus capex and insurance recommendations, with a portfolio dashboard for bond analysts.
why_now: Record occupancy and accelerating investment mean a wave of acquisitions and new starts is coming. The Colorado River decision framework landed in Aug 2026, PFAS monitoring starts in 2027, and Texas's data-center water crackdown showed water is now an explicit siting factor.
revenue_model: Per-report fees of $4-12k, annual subscriptions of $25-60k for bond funds and lender credit desks, and remediation referral fees from the sensor and water-treatment vendors that fix the flagged items.
non_obvious_insight: For senior housing, water risk is life-safety, not just cost. Residents cannot leave and the pathogens are lethal, so it should be underwritten like fire risk, yet nobody sells the underwriting standard. The first credible grade becomes the lender checklist item.
first_30_days: Publish a free water-risk map of the 60 largest CCRC and senior-housing bond issuers in Colorado River, Texas and Florida stress zones. Email it to 30 muni analysts and 10 HUD lenders, and offer three discounted deal reports at $3k.

title: Men's Repair Crews Funded by Aging-in-Place Budgets
one_liner: A membership club for men 25-45 who show up weekly to do minor home repairs for isolated older adults, led by a paid tradesperson and paid for by aging-in-place budgets.
customer: Payers are Medicare Advantage plans (home-safety supplemental benefits), Area Agencies on Aging, city aging-in-place funds and Medicaid home-modification programs, paying $400-900 per job. Members add about $30 a month in dues.
problem: Men reject talk-based loneliness solutions, and therapy framing fails them. Men's Sheds show that shoulder-to-shoulder tasks build belonging (97% of members in one survey said they have a place where they belong), but they run on charity money. Meanwhile older adults with unfixed stairs, missing grab bars and poor lighting fall, and licensed repair labor for small jobs is scarce and expensive.
solution: Crews of 8-10 men with one paid licensed lead. A 3-hour Saturday job (grab bars, rails, ramps, lighting, smoke alarms) followed by a shared meal. Rotating pairs do check-in visits. Software handles referral intake from care managers, photo scoping, materials, volunteer liability coverage, and payer invoicing with before/after proof and a fall-risk checklist.
why_now: Male loneliness is now a headline metric (WHO commission, Jun 2025) but products remain talk-based. Medicare Advantage plans are under margin pressure and favor cheap benefits with hard outcomes such as fall prevention. Programs modeled on CAPABLE (repairs plus clinician visits) have shown large drops in daily-living disability. Trades labor is short.
revenue_model: Per-job fees from payers ($400-900), member dues, and materials sponsorship from hardware retailers. Volunteer labor makes the gross margin work. Later: employer-sponsored membership.
non_obvious_insight: Men join for a task, not a talk, so give them a task that a payer already funds and cannot staff. The 'male loneliness' problem and the 'home-modification labor shortage' are the same market seen from two sides.
first_30_days: Partner with one Area Agency on Aging or a Rebuilding Together affiliate that already has a waitlist of households. Recruit 8 men via a local run club, climbing gym and Reddit. Hire a retired contractor as lead at about $40 an hour. Complete 4 pilot jobs at $350 each, document outcomes, and pitch two Medicare Advantage care-management teams with the first 20 jobs.

title: Outside-Processing Milk Run for Job Shops
one_liner: Scheduled pickup routes and batching software for the heat-treat, plating and anodize bottleneck behind reshored machining.
customer: 10-100 person machine shops and fabricators, plus special-process houses (heat treat, anodize, plating, passivation, paint) that want fuller batches.
problem: As machining orders rise (machinery jobs +6.1k in August, record capital-goods orders), the constraint moves downstream to special processes. Shops ship parts by carrier ad hoc, parts sit in queues, and paperwork gets lost. ISM supplier deliveries have slowed for eight straight months. Environmental cost and owner retirements limit new special-process capacity (my inference).
solution: Vans on fixed weekly or daily routes between shops and vetted process vendors. Batching gives vendors full loads. Barcode chain of custody carries cert paperwork (heat-treat charts, NADCAP status). A promised turnaround (for example 5 days) is tracked by software.
why_now: Reshoring in existing walls raises job counts while outside-process capacity has not grown. Slowing deliveries make lead time visible.
revenue_model: Per-stop fee plus 8-12% margin on outside-processing volume. Vendor SaaS. Later, acquire a heat-treat or anodize house.
non_obvious_insight: Outside processing often accounts for most of a job's elapsed lead time but only a small share of touch time. That bottleneck yields to logistics and batching, not new furnaces, and adding a van is cheaper than adding an oven.
first_30_days: Pick one region such as Grand Rapids, Greenville or Wichita. Interview 20 shops. Sign two heat-treat or anodize houses. Run a one-van pilot two days a week and charge per stop.

title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.

title: WhatsApp Tandas With Credit Reporting
one_liner: Felix proved WhatsApp-native finance at $8B of volume. Wrap the rotating savings groups that immigrant households already run in group chats with escrow, default cover and credit reporting.
customer: Latino, West African, Caribbean and South Asian households running tandas, susus and chit-fund-style rotating savings groups. The FDIC's 2023 survey counts 5.6M unbanked and 19M underbanked households, with minimum balances the top barrier.
problem: Rotating savings groups are the real financial system for many households, but they run on cash and trust, one bad organizer or defaulter breaks the pot, and the on-time payment history is invisible to credit bureaus. Cash-funded remittances now carry a 1% federal tax, nudging cash economies toward digital.
solution: A WhatsApp bot to create a tanda (amounts, order, schedule). Contributions are held in a partner-bank pass-through balance, or in stablecoin where appropriate, and payouts release on schedule. The organizer earns a fee, and a small guarantee pool covers late payers. On-time contributions are reported to bureaus as installment history through a furnisher partner.
why_now: Felix reached $8B cumulative volume with revenue up 2.5x on WhatsApp, the remittance tax pushes cash users to digital rails (Forbes, 2026-07-17), and stablecoin and bank-partner rails make small-balance escrow cheap.
revenue_model: 1-2% fee on each pot, $5 per month credit-building subscription, and lender referral fees for graduated members.
non_obvious_insight: Don't replace the tanda, wrap it. The organizer is a trusted social underwriter with better default data than any bureau. The pooled payment history of organized groups becomes a proprietary dataset lenders will pay for.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 organizers via Spanish-language WhatsApp and Facebook groups, churches, taquerias and community organizations. Run 10 pilot tandas with manual escrow in a partner-bank sub-account at a 1.5% fee, and validate the credit-reporting path with a furnisher.

title: Proof-of-Resident Public Comment
one_liner: Privacy-preserving verification that a public comment or 311 report comes from a real resident, without collecting their identity.
customer: City clerks, county boards, school districts, planning departments and state agencies running public-comment portals.
problem: Governments use GenAI to write documents, and vendors and activists use AI to flood the channels back. Councils and agencies can no longer tell 50 real residents from 5,000 bot-generated comments, so legitimate voices lose weight and hearings are contested.
solution: A comment widget that accepts a zero-knowledge proof from a mobile driver's license or wallet credential, proving residency and unique personhood without revealing name or address. Public dashboards show verified versus unverified counts, and the clerk keeps an audit log.
why_now: Mobile driver's licenses are live in a growing number of states, and wallet-level zero-knowledge proofs shipped in 2025. The signal-to-noise collapse from AI-generated submissions is now visible in procurement and public comment.
revenue_model: $5-30K per year per jurisdiction, with per-verification fees for state agencies and rulemaking dockets. Partner with agenda-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Verification without identity is the only approach that a hostile public will accept. Councils do not want a citizen database, they want a trustworthy count.
first_30_days: Build the widget with an open wallet-credential library in a state that supports mobile IDs. Pilot with one city clerk for a controversial hearing. Publish the verified-versus-unverified result.

title: Royalty-Paying Archive of Master Tradespeople's Hands
one_liner: Pay retiring master electricians, pipefitters and welders to record expert egocentric video with think-aloud narration, license it to robotics companies, and share royalties with the workers.
customer: Robotics and embodied-AI companies building construction, maintenance and data center installation robots, and foundation-model labs. A second buyer is apprenticeship programs and trade schools, which can license the annotated footage as curriculum.
problem: Egocentric data for robots is being commoditized at the bottom: in September 2026 reporting, gig workers earn about $3-10 an hour filming dishwashing and folding laundry. Expert tasks, like reading a bad splice or feeling a torque, are rare in the data, and the people who know them are retiring, which is also the labor shortage the AI buildout depends on.
solution: Recruit 60+ year-old tradespeople through union retiree halls. Pay $60-120 an hour to wear head and wrist cameras (plus IMU gloves) on real jobs with owner consent, and to narrate why they choose each action and how they detect problems. Add edge-case tagging by a second expert. Blur faces and PII. License datasets by the hour, and pay each worker a royalty of 10-20% of license revenue and a residual on repeat licensing.
why_now: In 2026 papers such as EgoHumanoid showed that robot-free human egocentric demonstrations can train humanoid manipulation directly, so human video is now a working input. The commodity layer is crowded and cheap, so expert-conditioned data is the next premium. Labor and IP disputes over gig data are also starting, which makes a royalty model a moat.
revenue_model: License $150-600 per hour of expert-annotated footage (a hypothesis to test in pilots), exclusivity premiums, and pre-paid data collection contracts. Secondary revenue from trade-school curriculum licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Robotics' bottleneck is shifting from quantity to tacit expertise, and tacit expertise is a wasting asset because its holders are retiring. A royalty share turns those workers from data laborers into stakeholders, which is a legal, ethical and recruiting advantage the $3-an-hour vendors cannot copy.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 retired electricians and pipefitters via IBEW and UA retiree halls and local Facebook groups. Get two robotics startups to pre-pay $25-50k each for 100 hours. Equip people with a $400 kit and a one-page site consent and PII-blur workflow. Deliver the first 20 hours with narration and get a written reference from each buyer.

title: Concession-Adjusted Comps for Appraisers
one_liner: A browser tool that reconstructs what homes really sold for after seller credits and buydowns, so appraisers, lenders and AVMs stop valuing collateral off gross headline prices.
customer: Independent residential appraisers and small appraisal firms in high-concession metros (Atlanta, Austin, Dallas, Phoenix, Florida) first; then appraisal management companies, HELOC/home-equity lenders and AVM vendors.
problem: Redfin reports 44.7% of Aug 2026 sales carried seller concessions (Atlanta 72.8%) while national price indices still show +3.7% YoY. The recorded price is gross; the credit or rate buydown lives in MLS remarks, agent notes and the Closing Disclosure. Appraisers are expected to adjust comps for concessions but have no reliable data, so they burn hours phoning agents, and collateral values drift above true net prices.
solution: A Chrome/desktop add-on that runs inside the appraiser's own MLS session. It uses LLM extraction over listing remarks, price history and agent notes to estimate concession type and dollar value (closing-cost credit, 2-1 buydown cost, permanent points), asks the appraiser to confirm with a one-click agent email, and writes a supported adjustment into the sales-comparison grid. Confirmed records build a cooperative net-price database, later licensed as an index and API.
why_now: Record concession share with 30-year rates near 7.5% has made seller-funded buydowns a de facto financing product. Structured appraisal reporting makes concession fields explicit, and LLMs only recently became reliable at parsing messy MLS remarks.
revenue_model: $49-79 per appraiser seat per month; site licenses for AMCs and lenders; net-price index and API licensed to AVM vendors and home-equity portfolios ($0.10-0.50 per lookup or an annual data license).
non_obvious_insight: Sellers defend the headline price and negotiate the credit, so the true markdown is invisible in every public index and owned by nobody. Appraisers feel this pain daily, which gives a labeled, growing dataset for free and a wedge into lenders whose collateral models are quietly overstated.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 appraisers from state appraiser groups in Atlanta and Austin. Ship a remarks-parsing concession worksheet as an MVP with a 2-week trial, then charge $49 per month. Publish a monthly 'net vs recorded price' note for five metros to get press and lender attention. Stay within each appraiser's own MLS license and do no bulk scraping.

title: Laid-Off Auto Technicians to Water Operators
one_liner: A paid-placement training pipeline that turns displaced auto and machinery technicians into licensed water and wastewater operators.
customer: Contract water operators and small utilities, paying $4-8k per placed operator. State dislocated-worker and WIOA funds cover much of the tuition.
problem: Water systems face retirements, PFAS, nitrate and 2027 lead-and-copper deadlines with too few skilled operators. Meanwhile auto OEM robot orders are down 25% and autos lost 4.5k jobs in August, while the industrial maintenance and PLC skills those workers hold are what treatment plants cannot find.
solution: An 8-12 week bootcamp that maps PLC, pump, motor and controls skills onto Grade 1-2 operator exams plus PFAS media, ion exchange and membrane basics. Each trainee has a conditional job offer as an operator-in-training before starting. Solve the experience-hours bottleneck through contract-operator trainee slots.
why_now: Auto and metals layoffs are running alongside record capital-goods orders. Compliance clocks (PFAS monitoring 2027, LCRI Nov 2027) force hiring now, and EPA money for treatment is flowing.
revenue_model: Placement fee per hire from employers, plus state workforce-fund tuition reimbursement. Optional income-share for trainees.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint on water treatment is not money. It is people who can keep a PLC-run plant alive, and shrinking auto plants hold exactly those people.
first_30_days: Contact state Rapid Response teams for two Midwest auto-plant layoffs. Sign one contract operator for 10 conditional offers. Run a first cohort of 12 with a community-college partner.

title: Muscle Ultrasound Scans as a Gym Vital Sign
one_liner: A five-minute, AI-read thigh ultrasound that tells GLP-1 users and lifters whether they are keeping their muscle.
customer: Gyms, GLP-1 and weight-loss clinics and PT clinics; consumers pay $29-49 per scan, clinics pay per-scan licenses.
problem: Studies suggest 20-50 percent of weight lost on GLP-1 drugs can be lean mass, but scales, bioimpedance and photos cannot show muscle and DEXA is costly and inconvenient. Trainers and clinics have no cheap, objective muscle metric to motivate clients or steer dosing and training.
solution: A coach scans the quadriceps with a handheld probe; AI segments rectus femoris and vastus intermedius thickness and echogenicity; results are trended over time and against a cohort. Positioned as general wellness muscle-thickness tracking that integrates with training and nutrition plans, not diagnosis.
why_now: Handheld ultrasound now shows excellent agreement with cart systems for quadriceps thickness (ICC above 0.9 in a 2025 study), automated AI muscle segmentation is maturing, muscle loss on GLP-1s was a headline debate at ADA 2026, and the FDA's wellness posture is looser.
revenue_model: $29-49 per scan retail; gym device-plus-software rental at $299-499 per month; per-scan fees for clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Trend in thickness, not absolute mass, is precise enough to change behavior. It is a retention and upsell tool for gyms (more strength coaching for people who can see the muscle they are protecting).
first_30_days: Buy two handheld probes, validate against DEXA on 50 volunteers with a partner clinic, run scan days at three gyms and one GLP-1 clinic at $39 per scan, and sign the first monthly device subscription.

title: Powered Public Land Brokerage for Robotaxi Depots
one_liner: A broker that matches autonomous-fleet operators to cities' already-energized, under-used land such as transit depots, fleet yards and city garages, on leases that trade concessions cities value.
customer: Robotaxi, autonomous delivery-van and driverless-truck operators pay success fees and retainers (Waymo, Zoox, May Mobility, Avride, Gatik and others). Cities and transit agencies are the counterparty, earning lease income.
problem: Depot power is the choke point for scaling robotaxis. A standard California charging site takes about 6 months, a new circuit 1.9 years, a substation upgrade 2.8 years and a new substation 8.9 years, and depots now compete with data centers for powered industrial land. Waymo's first 86M miles were only 54% passenger-carrying, so depots and reset cycles matter more than vehicles. AV operators do not know which public parcels are already energized, because they sit in transit-agency asset registers rather than commercial real estate databases.
solution: Build a dataset of municipally owned parcels with existing high-capacity service: bus depots, municipal fleet yards, park-and-ride lots, closed school-bus yards, airport lots and city garages. Overlay it with utility load-capacity maps. Use a template 'public benefit lease' (revenue share, 24/7 emergency access, data sharing, wheelchair-accessible service commitments, local cleaning and charging jobs) so cities can say yes without a full RFP. Then broker the deals.
why_now: Waymo raised $16B at a $126B valuation in Feb 2026 and is expanding across 10-14 metros. Zoox began charging fares on Aug 10, 2026, Tesla is running unsupervised in two states, and Aurora is exiting 2026 with 200 driverless trucks that need terminals. Large-load grid queues are freezing in Texas, so already-energized land is worth years.
revenue_model: A success fee of 3-5% of lease value or $75-150k per signed site, plus $10-20k/month retainers from fleets that want a standing pipeline. Optional revenue share with the city.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input for autonomous-fleet scale is already-energized land, not compute or vehicles, and the largest holder of it is city government. City government cannot run a competitive marketplace but values non-cash concessions (accessibility, data, jobs) that a private landlord never offers.
first_30_days: In Texas, Arizona and Georgia metros with announced AV expansions, file public-records requests for depot and yard inventories plus utility service sizes. Build a 100-parcel shortlist. Pitch three fleet real-estate leads a paid $25k 'top-10 sites' report.

title: Frozen Models: Long-Term Support for AI Deployments
one_liner: A 'Red Hat for AI models': host specific model versions with a written 5-7 year availability guarantee, reproducibility pack and migration diff-testing, for companies that cannot let their AI change under them.
customer: Model-risk, compliance and QA leads at mid-size banks, insurers, health-tech and pharma-adjacent firms, and legal-tech teams that have validated an AI workflow. Later, AI-companion products and their users, who care about persona continuity.
problem: Frontier labs retire models on 12-18 month cycles. Every retirement forces re-running evals, re-validating prompts and re-documenting for auditors. When OpenAI retired GPT-4o from ChatGPT on Feb 13, 2026, it set off the #Keep4o backlash, proving people and firms treat model behavior as something they depend on.
solution: Pin and host frozen snapshots of open-weight models (and customers' own fine-tunes), with contractual availability through a stated year, a fixed and documented inference stack (versions, quantization, seeds), and a change-control pack (model card, eval suite, audit logs). Add a migration service that replays your real traffic through old and new models and produces a behavior-diff report when you choose to upgrade.
why_now: Deprecation cycles have shortened and the 2026 GPT-4o episode made instability visible outside engineering teams. Regulators and auditors increasingly ask for documented change control on AI systems, and open-weight models are now good enough for many bounded enterprise tasks. Nobody is selling stability itself as the product.
revenue_model: Monthly hosting subscription plus per-token usage, one-time change-control pack fees, and per-migration diff-testing engagements.
non_obvious_insight: Enterprises don't buy the best model, they buy the model that won't change. Each frontier release is a validation event for regulated buyers, so a vendor whose product is boring stability (like Ubuntu LTS or RHEL) has a natural niche, and the cost side is cheap because old open weights run on modest GPUs. The consumer angle (keeping a beloved persona alive) adds emotional stickiness that pure infra players can't match.
first_30_days: Interview 20 model-risk and compliance leads in banks and insurers. Publish a one-page 'frozen model SLA' with pricing. Host three open-weight snapshots on rented GPUs with a documented inference stack. Close two design partners at $2-5k/month and produce the first reproducibility pack.

title: ZIP-Level Appetite Radar for Distressed Markets
one_liner: A live map of which carriers are actually binding homes in which distressed ZIPs, sold to agents and to carriers owing coverage quotas.
customer: Independent agents and wholesale brokers in California (then Florida and Colorado). Carriers pay for pre-qualified submissions in ZIPs where they owe quota.
problem: The CA FAIR Plan hit 696,562 policies (up 8% since Sept 2025) and raised rates about 29.1%. Under the Sustainable Insurance Strategy, carriers get rate freedom in exchange for an 85% writing commitment in distressed ZIPs. Zurich, Mercury and CSAA say they are expanding, yet the June 2026 regulator release gave no numbers. Agents burn hours on declines, and nobody can see the ZIP-by-ZIP flip.
solution: Combine agent-contributed anonymized quote outcomes, licensed quote probing and rate/rule filing monitoring. Publish which carriers bind in each ZIP by roof age and mitigation class, with estimated savings versus FAIR. Agents get a 'who will write this' answer in seconds. Carriers pay a bounty per bound policy.
why_now: California's rewritten rulebook took effect in 2026 while regulator disclosure stayed opaque, so the information gap is largest now.
revenue_model: $99-249/month per agent, plus $75-200 carrier bounties per bound policy.
non_obvious_insight: Headlines say California is broken, but reality is a patchwork flipping ZIP by ZIP. Carriers with quota obligations are price-insensitive buyers of distribution, and agents are blind to them.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 independent agencies in wildfire-adjacent counties to a shared outcome log (a form and spreadsheet is enough). Publish a weekly 'who is writing' report and start charging at week four.

title: The True Acceptance Map for Rural Transfers
one_liner: Voice AI agents call every receiving psychiatric unit and specialty hospital each night to learn what they will actually accept, and rural ERs text a number to find out who will say yes.
customer: Critical access hospital EDs, state hospital associations and state rural health offices (paid with Rural Health Transformation Program funds), and state behavioral health authorities. Subscription per hospital or per state.
problem: A rural ER holding a suicidal 16-year-old, or a stroke, trauma or OB patient, may spend 3-8 hours making phone calls to place them. State bed registries say beds are open, but the real decision is made by a house supervisor at 2am applying unwritten rules: no IV drug history, no one-to-one sitter, no autism, no patients over 250 lb, no out-of-state Medicaid, no aggression, and no calls after 9pm without a physician-to-physician call. Every ER charge nurse keeps a battered binder or a phone note of who says yes to what and who to ask for. It lives in one head, and it goes out of date when a house supervisor changes.
solution: Use voice agents to call each facility's intake line on a schedule and extract structured, current answers: true open capacity by population, unwritten exclusions, insurance rules, the name and direct number of the person who decides, and the hours that person answers. Serve it back through a plain SMS interface. A nurse texts 'psych, 16yo, Medicaid, sitter needed, hx cutting' and gets a ranked call list with the exact script to use (the words that get an acceptance). Only facility rules are collected. No patient data is ever in the calls. Later, sell a receiving-side listing so facilities can pre-qualify referrals and get fewer dead-end calls.
why_now: Every state has now posted Rural Health Transformation Program funding opportunities (as of August 2026), and care coordination and access technology are core uses. Research on bed-tracking systems shows registries still leave clinicians phoning to check appropriateness, especially for aggressive, medically complex, autistic and dementia patients. Voice agents from 2025-26 can now hold a natural two-minute call with an intake nurse for a few cents. The workforce shortage means intake lines are answered by fewer people, which makes the tacit rules more valuable.
revenue_model: $300-600 per ER per month for SMS access. State-level licenses of $100-300k per year paid from RHTP or behavioral health funds. A second line is a receiving-facility listing at about $500 per month per facility. The proprietary asset is a data graph of real rules that no registry has.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable data is not bed counts, which are wrong within an hour. It is the tacit acceptance criteria and the identity of the human who decides, and it can only be learned by phone at night. That is why bed-registry vendors (built on hospital self-reporting) miss it. Facilities that discover their rules are being published accurately will cooperate, because a dead-end call costs them time too.
first_30_days: Pick one state or region. Type up the founder nurse's own binder, about 60-80 facilities, into a spreadsheet. Wire an off-the-shelf voice agent platform to call each facility nightly and write results to a table. Put an SMS bot in front of it with a Twilio number. Give it free to five ERs in the region and compare call counts and time to placement before and after. Bring the numbers to the state hospital association and the RHTP office.

title: Injection-Proof Video Calls for High-Stakes Approvals
one_liner: A WebRTC layer that accepts only video frames attested by the phone's secure hardware, killing virtual-camera and deepfake injection in notarizations and wire approvals.
customer: Remote online notarization platforms, title and escrow firms, banks' high-value approval calls, and later IDV vendors.
problem: Deepfake injection through virtual cameras, emulators and rooted devices defeats isolated liveness checks and video ID. Detection is a statistical arms race that decays with each new generator.
solution: An Android-first SDK and server verifier that checks device and app attestation (Key Attestation and Play Integrity, and App Attest on iOS for app integrity). Where the hardware supports it, it uses signed capture, then verifies that a session's frames come from an unmodified device and camera pipeline. It flags emulators and virtual cameras and runs beneath existing call providers.
why_now: Flagship phones now sign captured media (Pixel 10 Content Credentials, Samsung Galaxy S25 for AI edits). Injection attacks are now the standard route around IDV, and the CEN/TS 18099 injection-attack standard gives buyers a language for it.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.50 per attested session plus $2-10K per month platform fees.
non_obvious_insight: Detecting fakes is a losing game, while attesting the camera turns it into a cryptographic one. You do not need to sign the world's video, only the few sessions that move money or property.
first_30_days: Build the Android SDK and a demo, publish a red-team result against a virtual camera, approach 5 RON providers and title-tech firms, and run 3 paid pilots at about $2K per month.

title: Operator-of-Record for Enterprise Drone Flights
one_liner: A licensed BVLOS operations team-as-a-service that files the waivers, runs the safety case and supervises the flights for utilities, solar developers and pipeline owners.
customer: Mid-size utilities and co-ops, solar and wind developers, pipeline and rail operators, ports, mines, and their insurers.
problem: BVLOS technology is ready, but organizations lack the capability: waiver applications, safety cases, ops manuals, remote-pilot staffing and data pipelines. The final status of Part 108 (the FAA BVLOS rule) could not be verified, which adds uncertainty. Meanwhile the DJI ban forces fleet refreshes.
solution: A reusable safety-case library and remote-pilot center (one pilot supervising 5-10 drone docks) running US-made drone-in-a-box fleets. Price per line-mile or per site, with data delivered into the customer's GIS and maintenance systems.
why_now: The December 2025 DJI restrictions force fleet replacement decisions in 2026, and Wing's 1M deliveries show BVLOS operations working at scale. Whatever Part 108's final form, operators still need documented safety cases and waivers.
revenue_model: $5-20k per month per site retainer or per-line-mile pricing on multi-year MSAs, plus waiver and safety-case consulting fees.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation is a one-time cost that vendors avoid, but the operator-of-record that accumulates waivers, flight logs and accepted safety cases builds a moat that compounds with every approval.
first_30_days: Pick one region (for example co-ops in Texas or Colorado) and partner with one US-made dock vendor. Get one co-op to sign a pilot covering 20 substations, file the waiver, and aim for the first inspection within 60 days.

title: AI-Run Cardiometabolic Care at ACCESS Prices
one_liner: An AI-first, pharmacist-supervised chronic-care program engineered to profit at Medicare ACCESS payment rates that break human-coach models.
customer: CMS pays it as an ACCESS participant ($360 per beneficiary per year initially, $180 follow-on, with half withheld pending outcomes). Medicare beneficiaries enroll at no cost. Later Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans pay.
problem: ACCESS launched Jul 5, 2026 with ~150 participants. Payment works out to ~$30/month and Omada and Hinge sat out, so incumbents' cost structures don't fit. Primary care cannot titrate hypertension, lipid and prediabetes meds for millions of patients at this price.
solution: A mailed validated BP cuff and scale, voice-AI check-ins, protocolized titration of low-cost generics (ARB or CCB, statin, ezetimibe, metformin) and low-dose oral GLP-1 maintenance. Pharmacist and NP co-sign changes, with autonomous renewals only where state sandboxes allow (Utah's Jan 2026 AI renewal pilot covers 190 meds but excludes injectables and controlled substances).
why_now: ACCESS is live with rolling cohorts and a Jan 1, 2027 start. Oral GLP-1s are now first-line accessible, real-time voice AI is deployable, and a state has legally let AI renew chronic prescriptions.
revenue_model: CMS outcome-aligned payments of $360/year initial and $180/year follow-on per beneficiary. Target unit cost under ~$150/year for 50%+ margin, plus outcome-linked upside.
non_obvious_insight: At $30 per member per month the winner is whoever gets cost per member under about $12/month, which is an AI-to-pharmacist ratio problem, not a product problem. Big digital-health brands are structurally excluded.
first_30_days: Confirm the current CMS application window for the Jan 1, 2027 cohort. Meanwhile pilot 200 cash or MA patients with cheap cuff kits through a partner pharmacy, measure BP control and unit cost, and recruit a pharmacist supervisor and medical director.

title: Builder Defect Outbreak Radar From Permit Clusters
one_liner: Epidemiology for houses: read repair-permit clusters by builder, subdivision and vintage to tell HOA boards they have a defect outbreak and how many months remain on the legal clock.
customer: HOA management companies and reserve-study firms (about $99-250 per community per year, or a $750 one-time scan). Independent home inspectors and buyer's agents in new-build subdivisions ($19-39 per address). Later, home-warranty companies and homeowners insurers as data licensees.
problem: Production-home defects (roofs, windows, stucco or siding, plumbing, foundations) show up as patterns, but each owner sees only their own house. Boards learn late. Statutes of repose and limitation for construction-defect claims typically run roughly 6-10 years depending on state and quietly expire. Buyers pay for the defect discount without knowing why, and the MLS says nothing.
solution: Ingest city and county permit data. Use an LLM to classify messy permit text (re-roof, window replacement, siding or stucco remediation, re-pipe, foundation or pier repair, water-intrusion repair). Tie parcels to subdivision, builder and year built from plat and assessor data. Compare repair-permit rates to age-matched control cohorts in the same metro. Flag statistically significant outliers. Deliver a 'Community Defect Scan': map, cohort comparison, estimated time left under the applicable state statute (information, not legal advice), and next steps (independent engineer, reserve study update, attorney consult). Also offer a per-address flag API for inspectors.
why_now: The 2020-2022 building boom, built under labor and material shortages with substitutions, is now 4-6 years old, when defects surface and the earliest repose clocks start closing. Permit portals and open data are far more digitized than five years ago. LLMs make classification of messy permit text nearly free. Insurers and lenders are increasingly sensitive to new-build condition.
revenue_model: Community scans at $750 one-time. Management-company portfolio subscriptions at $99-250 per community per year. Per-address inspector add-on at $19-39. Data licensing to warranty and insurance underwriters. Flat fees only, with no referral fees to law firms, to avoid fee-splitting problems.
non_obvious_insight: Individual defects are invisible, but outbreaks are not. Appraisers watch this pattern for years without a feed: neighbors all re-roofing in year 5, three permits for the same water-intrusion fix on one street. The payer isn't the buyer, it's the board with a ticking legal deadline and a manager who wants to look proactive. The trick that makes a 'builder X is an outlier' claim defensible is controlling for age, since old-house repairs are normal and only age-matched cohort comparison isolates the builder.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with clean open permit data and heavy 2019-22 production building (for example Denver suburbs, Phoenix East Valley or Austin/Round Rock). Build the pipeline over about 200 subdivisions. Produce 10 free scans for community managers. Have counsel review the wording (state permit counts and method only, no accusations). Pitch 5 management companies and 3 reserve-study firms, and sell the first 10 scans at $750.
